newsitem.title: GERMANY: Consensus culture works on Krupp, Thyssen.
newsitem.headline: Consensus culture works on Krupp, Thyssen.

text.p: Intervention by German politicians from all sides and resistance by Ruhr steelworkers were probably behind Krupp's move to postpone its hostile bid for steelmaker Thyssen, analysts said on Wednesday.

But given the consensus-building culture that pervades so much of German political and business life, the possibility cannot be ruled out that the conglomerate's original 14 billion mark ($8.4 billion) offer was only ever an elaborate bluff that has now succeeded in bringing Thyssen to the negotiating table.

"This is so typically German. It's as though they saw the worker demonstrations on Tuesday and then got round a table together with a glass of wine and said: 'Oh well, perhaps we can work out something together after all'," said Hans-Peter Wodniok, Frankfurt-based Credit Lyonnais analyst.
"Or you can speculate: Krupp decided to bring out the tanks just to get Thyssen talking to it," he added.

Accompanied by wine or not, discussions were held between Krupp and Thyssen on Tuesday evening "at the invitation" of North Rhine-Westphalia state premier Johannes Rau, the two groups confirmed on Wednesday.

Rau, who had publicly deplored the "Wild West" takeover bid, brought along to the talks both the finance and economic ministers of the Social Democratic-run region, home to much of Germany's industrial base.

This was where the decision was taken to explore the creation of a "commonly-held steel business", according to statements by Krupp, Thyssen and the state of North Rhine-Westphalia issued on Wednesday.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his economics minister Guenter Rexrodt later added their voices to a growing chorus of concern at the acute job losses that could result from a fusion of the two businesses.

"In the interest of those employed by both companies and in the interest of the economic climate in our country, the issue is to find a reasonable solution," Kohl was quoted as saying in an advance excerpt from Thursday's Bild newspaper.
Rexrodt urged the two to work towards an agreement that could help secure jobs in the steel sector in the long-term.
But what is unclear is to what extent Krupp expected -- or even banked on -- political pressure ultimately pushing the two companies into talks.
"That is the whole question -- did the pressure come from outside or was this all just a game of poker," said Markus Reichle the London-based German analyst with Paribas.

The most likely scenario, Reichle suggested, is that Krupp chief executive Gerhard Cromme launched the bid on Tuesday knowing full well that, one way or another, the two parties would at some stage be pushed into talking with each other.
Moreover, the eight-day breathing space now created by the talks throws up what could be a winning alternative strategy for Krupp, he added.
"If I were Cromme, I would start buying Thyssen shares while they are cheap on the grey market," Reichle said.

Earlier, dealers said Thyssen shares fell to 413 marks in unofficial trade after the announcement of the co-operation talks. Following suspension of Thyssen shares at 346.80 marks on Monday, they had risen to just below Krupp's offer price of 435 marks.

Acting in league with friendly banks Krupp could build up a stake above the five percent threshold at which stakes in other German companies are declarable. Such an announcement by Krupp could position it even better for an eventual takeover.
"But we have hardly ever seen anything like this before in Germany. It could be that people will look back at this and say that a completely new culture was in development," Reichle added.
